strengths: Introduces a simple and broadly applicable TD target modification, min(Q_target, Q_online), which is easy to integrate into value-based, distributional, offline, and actor-critic methods.
Provides extensive empirical evaluation across online/offline RL, discrete/continuous action spaces, and multiple algorithms, using Atari, MuJoCo, HBench, and DMC-Hard benchmarks.
Includes comparisons against relevant baselines such as Double DQN, FR-DQN, ScDQN, and Maxmin DQN, with careful metrics (IQM, AUC, confidence intervals) and multiple seeds.
The method requires no additional hyperparameters beyond the base algorithms and comes with a JAX code snippet and detailed hyperparameter tables, supporting reproducibility.
Provides a convergence argument by casting MINTO as a special case of the generalized Q-learning framework and verifying the required non-expansion conditions.
The operator ablation on Atari (Online Only, Target Only, Max, Mean, Random, Min) gives useful empirical support for the minimum operator over alternatives.
Demonstrates substantial gains in several settings, especially DQN/DQN-style Atari experiments and CQL offline RL, and shows improvements even on IQN and Simba-based continuous control.
The paper is generally clear, well-organized, and explicitly discusses limitations such as possible conservatism and future adaptive operator selection.
weaknesses: The core idea is incremental: taking the minimum between online and target estimates is closely related to existing conservative/min-based target constructions such as Maxmin Q-learning and Double Q-learning variants.

The theoretical analysis is limited: it is a direct corollary of an existing generalized Q-learning framework and does not address function approximation, replay, or the periodic target-network update scheme used in practice.

The claimed consistency across all benchmarks is somewhat overstated: on DMC-Hard, the method is comparable or slightly worse for SimbaV2, so the improvement is not uniform across continuous-control tasks.

The offline CQL+MINTO gain of roughly 125% in AUC with CNN is unusually large and would benefit from deeper investigation, such as sensitivity to CQL regularization and dataset/network choices, to rule out baseline under-tuning.
There is no direct empirical measurement of overestimation bias or moving-target reduction; the paper mainly relies on final performance and selection ratios for one game (Breakout).
The target-update frequency is fixed, but min-based bootstrapping may interact strongly with target update frequency; an ablation or sensitivity analysis is missing.
The computational overhead of an additional online forward pass on the next state is asserted to be negligible but not quantified in runtime or wall-clock terms.
The experimental evaluation on Atari uses a selected 15-game subset rather than the full suite, which is acceptable but limits the strength of the broad-applicability claim.

strengths: Simple, lightweight target update that is easy to integrate into existing algorithms and adds no new hyperparameters.
Extensive empirical evaluation across online/offline RL, discrete/continuous control, multiple algorithms (DQN, IQN, CQL, SAC/Simba), architectures, benchmarks, and seeds.
The operator comparison on 15 Atari games supports the proposed minimum criterion over alternatives and illustrates the instability of online-only bootstrapping.
Writing is generally clear and the related work positioning is helpful.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: taking the minimum of online and target estimates is a straightforward combination of existing ideas such as Maxmin Q-learning and Double Q-learning, and the theoretical result is essentially a direct corollary with a trivial non-expansion proof.

The convergence analysis is restricted to the tabular setting and does not provide insight into why MINTO stabilizes deep RL or how it interacts with function approximation, underestimation, and exploration.
Missing key ablation: no comparison to target networks with varying update frequencies, so it is unclear whether gains come from the minimum operator itself or simply from using less delayed targets.

Claims are stronger than the evidence: DMC-Hard results are comparable or worse for SimbaV2, contradicting statements that MINTO consistently improves across all benchmarks; the very large offline CQL gains are also not sufficiently explained.
Evaluation lacks stronger modern baselines in continuous control (e.g., CrossQ, REDQ, DroQ) and does not measure value bias directly to substantiate the overestimation argument.
Some design choices, such as using a single critic for SAC/Simba and relegating twin-critic results to the appendix, are not fully justified.
Reproducibility is partially limited: the full codebase is not yet released, only a JAX snippet is provided, and some hyperparameter/epoch accounting is ambiguous.

strengths: Proposes a simple, plug-and-play target computation rule that can be integrated into value-based, distributional, and actor-critic methods with negligible overhead and no additional hyperparameters.

Provides an extensive empirical evaluation across online/offline RL, discrete/continuous action spaces, multiple architectures (CNN, IMPALA+LN, SimbaV1/V2), and diverse benchmarks (Atari, MuJoCo, HumanoidBench, DMC-Hard).

Consistently improves performance over strong baselines in many settings, including DQN, IQN, CQL, SimbaV1, and SimbaV2, with meaningful gains in sample efficiency and asymptotic return on several benchmarks.
Includes a targeted ablation study comparing the minimum operator against alternative operators (max, mean, random, online-only, target-only), supporting the design choice empirically.
Provides a convergence analysis in the tabular setting by casting MINTO as a special case of the Generalized Q-learning framework, with a proof in the appendix.
The method is computationally lightweight, requiring only one additional feedforward pass on the next state, and the JAX snippet/pseudocode makes integration straightforward.
The paper is generally clear, well-motivated, and includes detailed hyperparameter settings and reproducibility statements.
weaknesses: The core idea—taking the minimum between online and target estimates—is simple and somewhat incremental relative to existing conservative/minimum-based target methods such as Maxmin Q-learning and self-correcting Q-learning.

The theoretical analysis is limited to the tabular setting and relies on conditions from Maxmin Q-learning; it does not directly address the deep RL setting with function approximation, target networks, or moving-target dynamics.

The claimed mechanism of 'faster learning via fresher online estimates' is not fully disentangled from a possible conservative underestimation/regularization effect, since the min operator can only lower the target relative to the target network.
Empirical improvements are not uniform: gains are modest for IQN (~7%) and absent or slightly negative on DMC-Hard for SimbaV2, yet these cases are not analyzed in depth.

The paper does not provide a detailed bias/variance or overestimation analysis across tasks; evidence for mitigating overestimation is mostly indirect through operator ablations and one online-selection curve.
Code is only promised upon acceptance, not currently available, which limits immediate reproducibility despite the provided pseudocode and hyperparameters.
Some design details, such as the interaction with exploration and the effect of applying MINTO to twin-critic actor-critic setups, are discussed only briefly or deferred to the appendix.

strengths: Proposes a simple, general, and easy-to-implement modification to TD targets: taking the minimum of target-network and online-network estimates. This can be integrated into many value-based and actor-critic algorithms with minimal code changes.
Provides broad empirical evidence across online RL, offline RL, discrete action spaces, and continuous control, including DQN, IQN, CQL, and SAC/Simba variants.
Includes an ablation over target-combination operators (Online Only, Target Only, Max, Mean, Random, Min) that supports the empirical choice of the minimum operator.
Introduces no additional hyperparameters, which is attractive for practical adoption and fair comparison.
Reports standard aggregate metrics (IQM, confidence intervals, AUC) and releases code/pseudocode, supporting reproducibility.
Provides a tabular convergence argument by casting MINTO as a special case of the Generalized Q-learning framework of Lan et al. (2020).
weaknesses: The core idea is conceptually incremental: combining online and target estimates via a minimum operator is closely related to existing ideas such as Maxmin Q-learning, clipped double Q-learning, and prior hybrid target/online methods. The paper does not establish a fundamentally new mechanism.

The theoretical contribution is limited: Corollary 1 is essentially a direct application of prior convergence results for Generalized Q-learning, restricted to the tabular setting, with no finite-sample analysis or function-approximation guarantees. The mapping from online/target networks to historical time indices is also somewhat informal.

The empirical evaluation, while broad, is not comprehensive: Atari experiments use only 15 games rather than the full 57-game suite, and results are often reported as percentage improvements over baselines without absolute normalized scores. This makes it harder to judge practical significance and variance.

Some claims of consistent improvement are overstated: in continuous control on DMC-Hard, gains are comparable or slightly lower for SimbaV2, and IQN gains are relatively modest. The paper would benefit from a more careful discussion of when MINTO is not beneficial.

The overhead of MINTO is described as negligible, but no wall-clock, FLOP, or memory analysis is provided. Since MINTO requires an additional online-network forward pass on next states, its practical cost should be quantified.

There is limited analysis of why the minimum operator works beyond mitigating overestimation, and little investigation into interactions with exploration, target update frequency, or low-noise environments where conservatism may hurt.

Some comparisons and implementation details are not fully transparent: the code release URL appears missing in the manuscript, and tuning procedures for baselines such as FR-DQN, ScDQN, and Maxmin methods are not described in detail.

The paper does not fully position MINTO against the most recent target-free or target-regularization methods, nor does it provide a clear decision rule for practitioners about when to prefer MINTO over existing target-network variants.

strengths: Simple, lightweight method that is easy to implement and requires no additional hyperparameters.
Broad empirical evaluation across online/offline RL, discrete/continuous control, value-based and actor-critic algorithms.
Includes an ablation over target operators and comparisons against several related baselines such as Double DQN, FR-DQN, ScDQN, and Maxmin DQN.
Provides a tabular convergence corollary showing MINTO fits the generalized Q-learning framework.
Appendix contains substantial implementation details, pseudocode, and individual per-environment results.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the proposed minimum operator is closely related to existing mechanisms such as clipped double Q-learning and Maxmin Q-learning; the key difference is using the online network as one of the two estimates, which is a small algorithmic change.

Theoretical analysis is weak: the convergence corollary is a straightforward application of Lan et al. (2020), does not analyze function approximation, and does not justify faster learning or reduced overestimation bias. The online and target estimates are highly correlated, so independence-based arguments from ensemble methods do not directly apply.

Empirical claims are overstated: MINTO does not consistently improve all benchmarks (e.g., DMC-Hard is comparable or slightly worse for SimbaV2), and the reported 125% AUC improvement for CQL+MINTO is suspiciously large and may indicate an under-tuned CQL baseline or implementation issue.

Experimental evaluation is not fully convincing: Atari results use only 15 games and 5 seeds, missing direct comparisons to simple two-critic min-based baselines in the DQN setting; offline RL gains are not sufficiently analyzed.

Reproducibility and clarity issues: the code URL is missing in the manuscript, some hyperparameters for CQL appear inherited from DQN settings without justification, and the paper contains notation errors and pseudocode inconsistencies.

The method lacks deeper analysis of when and why the minimum operator helps; the paper does not characterize the trade-off between underestimation, exploration, and stability beyond a limited Car-on-the-Hill study.

strengths: Simple, general, and easy-to-implement method that can be integrated into many value-based and actor-critic RL algorithms with minimal code changes and no additional hyperparameters.

Broad empirical evaluation spanning online/offline RL, discrete/continuous control, value-based/distributional/actor-critic methods, and multiple benchmarks, which provides good evidence of practical applicability.

The paper is clearly written, the motivation is well explained, and the method is intuitively appealing: using the online network only when it is more conservative than the target network reduces overestimation risk while retaining fresher estimates.
The theoretical convergence corollary, while limited, provides some formal grounding by connecting MINTO to the Generalized Q-learning/Maxmin Q-learning framework.
Reproducibility efforts are present, including released code, pseudocode, hyperparameter tables, and per-task results.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: taking a minimum between online and target estimates is closely related to existing ideas such as Maxmin Q-learning, clipped double Q-learning, self-correcting Q-learning, and functional-regularization approaches. The core contribution is a simple operator rather than a conceptually new mechanism.

The theoretical analysis is shallow: Corollary 1 is essentially a special case of existing generalized Q-learning results, focuses on tabular convergence, and does not address function approximation, target-network update schedules, or the coupled online/target dynamics in deep RL.

Evaluation concerns remain. In particular, the offline CQL experiments appear to use DQN/Dopamine-style hyperparameters rather than CQL-specific tuning, which raises the risk that the very large CQL+MINTO gains are partly due to an under-tuned baseline. This weakens the central offline RL claim.

The empirical improvement is not fully consistent: MINTO is comparable or slightly worse on DMC-Hard for SimbaV2, IQN gains are modest, and the paper’s claim of “consistently improves performance” is therefore somewhat overstated.

The interaction between MINTO and exploration, and the potential for overly conservative underestimation, is acknowledged but not analyzed. Since the method can dampen optimistic estimates, its behavior in sparse-reward or highly stochastic environments remains underexplored.

Atari evaluations use 15 games and 5 seeds, which is reasonable but still limited for strong generalization claims. Some reported gains may be sensitive to architecture, hyperparameters, and evaluation protocol.

The reproducibility statement appears to contain a missing/blank code link in the manuscript, and some implementation details depend on external codebases, which slightly weakens exact reproducibility.
